A Vintage
Bathroom.

Five photorealistic schemes drawn from one brief — Victorian bones, black and brass, mosaic underfoot — and tested against the room as it was actually measured.

Five schemes Room surveyed by 3D scan Brief by Mum
The brief, verbatim
1950s style vintage bathroom, with Victorian style toilet with pull chain, rolltop bath, glass shower screen with black beading, mosaic floor, black fittings, large deep wash basin, black iron radiator, chandelier, rounded mirror with wall mounted lights either side, brass fixtures.
— Mum
The room, as measured

Everything here has to fit a space
the size of a small box room.

5.69m² usable floor
1.84m wide — the bath wall
2.63m deep
2.365m ceiling
Lshaped — a corner is missing

These are real numbers, taken from wall planes in the 3D scan rather than guessed. The bath currently in the room measures exactly 1700 × 700 mm — a standard size — which is how we know the scan's scale is honest. The schemes below are style references, not to-scale renders: treat them as the feeling, and the survey as the fact.

What the brief really asks for

Decoded.

01

The list is Victorian, not 1950s.

Pull-chain high-level cisterns, roll-top baths, geometric mosaic and brass crossheads are Victorian and Edwardian — roughly 1837 to 1910. A genuine 1950s bathroom is a different room entirely: mint and pink pastels, chrome, checkerboard, a built-in bath. Both are lovely. They are not the same. Scheme 05 shows the actual 1950s version so the choice is made knowingly.

02

A roll-top and a shower screen fight each other.

A true freestanding roll-top wants 150–200 mm of clear space on every side, and a screen cannot seal against a curved rolled rim. In a 1.84 m alcove a 1700 mm roll-top leaves about 70 mm each side. The fix is well established: a back-to-wall or "shower" roll-top with one flat side, or drop to a 1500–1600 mm tub. Both keep the look.

03

Black and brass together is correct.

The working rule among designers is two finishes, three at most, with each repeated at least twice so it reads as intentional rather than accidental. Black behaves as a neutral and sits happily with brass. What matters is choosing a hero. Scheme 02 makes black the hero; Scheme 03 makes brass the hero. Both are shown so the difference is visible rather than theoretical.

04

The chandelier is a real detail, not a flourish.

With 2.365 m of headroom and a bath below, a hanging chandelier is a headroom and regulation problem. The answer is a semi-flush chandelier-style fitting, correctly IP-rated for its zone. It reads exactly the same from the doorway — which is where anyone will actually see it.

The five
01The Green Drawing RoomThe brief, literally 02The MonochromeBlack as hero 03Brass & BoneBest fit for the room 04The Jewel BoxThe bold one 05The MintActually 1950s
01The Green Drawing Room The brief, taken literally

Every item on the brief, present and correct. White bevelled metro tiles run to dado height with a moulded rail; above them the walls turn deep heritage green, which is the colour Victorian bathrooms actually used once tiling stopped. The roll-top is gloss black with polished brass ball-and-claw feet, and the shower screen is clear glass with the slim black beading Mum asked for.

Underfoot, a proper Victorian geometric mosaic in black, white and soft terracotta with a running border — the detail that does most of the period work in the whole room. The high-level cistern with its pull chain and mahogany seat sits against the tiled wall, brass flush pipe exposed, exactly as it would have been.

A round brass mirror flanked by two brass wall lights, a black cast-iron column radiator with brass valves, and a small crystal chandelier finish it. This is the most faithful reading of the brief of the five.

Palette

The pieces

  • Black cast-iron roll-top, brass claw feet
  • High-level WC, pull chain, mahogany seat
  • Deep fireclay basin on full pedestal
  • Brass crosshead taps, exposed bottle trap
  • Geometric mosaic floor with border
  • Black cast-iron column radiator
  • Round brass mirror + two brass sconces

Rough cost

£7,500 – £9,500Period sanitaryware and real mosaic carry a premium over a standard suite.

Honest note. Deep green eats light, and this room has one small window. It will feel rich and enveloping rather than bright — lovely in the evening, darker on a grey morning. Worth seeing a large sample on the actual wall before committing.
02The Monochrome Black as the hero finish

This is what happens when "black fittings" is taken seriously rather than as an accent. Charcoal-black tongue-and-groove panelling runs to dado height, chalk-white plaster above, and every fitting in the room follows the panelling down into black — including the high-level cistern and its pull chain, which is an unusual and very striking piece.

The floor is a tight black-and-white star and hexagon mosaic, higher contrast and more graphic than Scheme 01. The basin sits on a slim black metal washstand rather than a pedestal, which keeps the floor visible and makes the room feel less crowded than it is.

Small aged-brass touches on the taps and mirror stop the whole thing going cold. That restraint is the trick: brass as seasoning, not as a second hero.

Palette

The pieces

  • Matt black roll-top, white enamel interior
  • Black high-level WC + black pull chain
  • Basin on slim black washstand frame
  • Matt black crossheads, black bottle trap
  • Black & white star mosaic floor
  • Black cast-iron column radiator
  • Round black mirror + black sconces

Rough cost

£7,000 – £9,000Black sanitaryware is often a special order — allow longer lead times.

Honest note. The most dramatic of the five and the most demanding. In 5.69 m² with one small window, this much black is a genuine commitment — it will read as a jewel-like, deliberately dark room. It also shows every water mark, so matt black brassware needs wiping rather than admiring.
03Brass & Bone The one that suits this room best

The same period vocabulary as Scheme 01, tuned for a small room with one window. Cream crackle-glaze metro to dado height, chalky limewash above, and a warm neutral mosaic in cream, putty and faded terracotta. Nothing is white and cold; nothing is dark.

Unlacquered aged brass is the hero and it appears everywhere — the roll-top's claw feet, the exposed shower riser and rose, the crossheads, the washstand frame, the mirror and both wall lights. The black beading on the shower screen is the single dark line in the room, which is exactly what makes it read.

The basin sits on a slim brass washstand with a marble top, which gives the "large deep basin" of the brief without the visual bulk of a pedestal, and leaves somewhere to put things — the thing small bathrooms always lack.

Palette

The pieces

  • White roll-top with aged brass claw feet
  • High-level WC, brass flush pipe, oak seat
  • Deep basin on brass + marble washstand
  • Unlacquered brass crossheads throughout
  • Warm neutral mosaic with fine border
  • Column radiator, brass valves
  • Round brass mirror + opal glass sconces

Rough cost

£7,000 – £9,000Unlacquered brass costs more up front and ages to a patina rather than staying bright.

Honest note. If you want one recommendation, this is it. It keeps every element of the brief while working with the room's real limitation — its size and its single window — instead of against it. Be aware that unlacquered brass is meant to tarnish; if Mum wants it permanently shiny, specify lacquered.
04The Jewel Box The bold one

Colour-drenching: walls, full-height panelling, cornice, ceiling and the bath itself all in the same deep oxblood. It sounds mad in a small room and it is the oldest trick there is for one — when every surface is the same colour, the eye stops finding the corners and the room loses its edges.

Aged brass does all the lifting against the burgundy: the claw feet, the flush pipe and chain, the crossheads, the ornate mirror, the amber-shaded sconces and a proper crystal chandelier throwing warm pools of light. The mosaic goes dark — black, deep red and cream.

This is the version that people remember. It is also the least forgiving of a bad decision, because the colour is the whole room rather than one wall of it.

Palette

The pieces

  • Oxblood roll-top, brass claw feet
  • Full-height moulded panelling, eggshell
  • High-level WC, walnut seat, brass chain
  • Deep basin on dark timber + marble stand
  • Dark geometric mosaic with ornate border
  • Black cast-iron radiator, brass valves
  • Crystal chandelier + amber glass sconces

Rough cost

£8,500 – £11,000Bespoke panelling and a painted bath are what push this above the others.

Honest note. Colour-drenching genuinely works in small rooms, but it lives or dies on the lighting — get the sconces and chandelier wrong and it goes from jewel box to cave. Budget properly for the electrics here, and expect it to need good artificial light even in the day.
05The Mint What 1950s actually looks like

Included deliberately. The brief said "1950s style vintage", and this is what a genuine 1950s British bathroom looked like: soft mint gloss tile to two-thirds height, a slim black pencil trim and bullnose capping, warm white above, and a black-and-white checkerboard floor laid on the diagonal.

The bath is built into the alcove with a rolled rim and a tiled panel rather than standing on feet. Fittings are polished chrome, not brass. The basin is a wide, deep pedestal with pillar taps. The round mirror and paired wall lights from the brief are still here — they were just as much a fifties fixture as a Victorian one.

Put next to the four above, it makes the decision easy: if this is the room Mum pictured, the other schemes are the wrong century. If it isn't, then the brief is Victorian and Scheme 01 or 03 is home.

Palette

The pieces

  • Built-in bath, rolled rim, tiled panel
  • Low-level WC, chrome lever, timber seat
  • Wide deep pedestal basin, pillar taps
  • Polished chrome throughout
  • Diagonal checkerboard floor
  • Slim column radiator, chrome valves
  • Round chrome mirror + opal sconces

Rough cost

£5,500 – £7,000The cheapest of the five — a built-in bath, standard WC and chrome all cost less.

Honest note. Also the most practical. A built-in bath with a screen is easier to seal, easier to clean and takes up less room than anything on feet, and chrome is cheaper and more forgiving than brass. If budget or practicality wins over romance, this is the sensible answer.
Before anything is ordered

Five things still to settle.

01

What is the corner block?

The scan shows a 0.88 × 1.65 m volume outside the room — most likely the airing cupboard. Until we know, no layout is safe. It may also be the answer to where storage goes.

02

Where is the soil pipe?

Measure from the corner to the centre of the WC waste. A high-level Victorian WC sits in a different spot to the current one, and moving a soil connection is the single biggest cost in any bathroom job.

03

Can the floor take a cast-iron bath?

A cast-iron roll-top full of water and a person is a serious point load on a 1954 timber first floor. Acrylic roll-tops look near-identical and weigh a fraction. Worth a builder's eye before choosing.

04

Lighting is notifiable work.

Chandelier, both sconces and the extractor all sit in a room with a bath, so it is Part P work: a registered electrician and a certificate, with the right IP rating for each zone.

05

Ventilation, not decoration.

Period rooms with lots of gloss tile and one small window show condensation fast. The extractor needs to meet the 15 l/s requirement — the least romantic line in the budget and the one that protects everything else in it.

Notes & sources

The five images are photorealistic visualisations generated to the brief, not photographs of the actual room, and not to its exact dimensions. Room measurements are real, taken from the Polycam scan of 27 July 2026. Costs are planning ranges for a UK job outside London and will move with specification and trade availability.
